item.title: Tiburon, Belvedere brace for El Niño, king tides
item.description: Tiburon and Belvedere are filling sandbag stations and readying a shared emergency center for a strong to very strong El Niño, and officials urge residents to prepare.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon and Belvedere are filling sandbag stations and readying a shared emergency center for a strong to very strong El Niño, and officials urge residents to prepare.

Tiburon and Belvedere are filling sandbag stations and readying a shared emergency operations center for a winter that forecasters expect to bring a strong to very strong El Niño, and officials say residents need to get ready too.

NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said Oct. 8 there is a “greater than an 83% chance” a strong to very strong El Niño lasts through January-March. It put the same 83% odds on October-December bringing an event stronger than any El Niño since 1950. Its next update is due Nov. 12.

NOAA’s Oct. 15 seasonal outlook gives much of California, and the West Coast as far north as the Oregon coast, elevated odds of above-normal rain from November through January, though with less confidence than for the Southeast.

The season’s highest tides are predicted Nov. 24-26, Dec. 22-25 and Jan. 20-22, topping out at 7.23 feet above the average daily low tide Dec. 24 at NOAA’s San Francisco gauge. Those predictions don’t account for weather, and actual tides have been running 6 inches to 1 foot higher, Steven Torrence, director of the county Office of Emergency Management, told the Belvedere-Tiburon Emergency Preparedness Council Oct. 20.

Marin supervisors proclaimed a countywide local emergency that day, Torrence said, and Tiburon declared its own the next night.

Both towns have warned that they can’t stop every flood, and they are asking residents to sign up for emergency alerts, stock supplies and plan how to get home or shelter in place.

At an Oct. 14 El Niño workshop at the Belvedere-Tiburon Library, Laurie Nilsen, the Tiburon Police Department’s emergency services coordinator for Tiburon and Belvedere, told the more than 30 attendees that the most important thing they could do is become part of the emergency-preparation effort, just as much as the public works, fire and police crews who respond.

“For every one of you that’s prepared and can take care of themselves, that’s one less person, one less household that we have to worry about,” Nilsen said.

item.title: Tiburon, Belvedere, Strawberry voters are weighing eight local contests, four local measures
item.description: Five candidates for three Tiburon Town Council seats and four for three Reed Union board seats head the peninsula’s Nov. 3 ballot, with six other races and four measures.
item.content:encoded:
Five candidates for three Tiburon Town Council seats and four for three Reed Union board seats head the peninsula’s Nov. 3 ballot, with six other races and four measures.

Five candidates for three Tiburon Town Council seats and four for three Reed Union School District board seats head the peninsula’s Nov. 3 local ballot, which also carries six other contested races and four local measures, including Reed Union’s $115 million bond.

Marin County elections officials began mailing ballots Oct. 5, and in-person voting is underway at the Marin County Civic Center. A vote center and an exterior drop box open Oct. 31 at Westminster Presbyterian Church in Tiburon, and the 24-hour drop box at Belvedere City Hall is already open. Both drop boxes close at 8 p.m. Election Day, Nov. 3, when every vote center is open 7 a.m.-8 p.m.

Not every race is on every ballot, and each section notes which voters decide it. The Ark’s full stories on most of these races and measures are at thearknewspaper.com/election2026. The state and federal contests ran in the Oct. 7 edition.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Town council, Tiburon voters

Mayor Jon Welner isn’t seeking reelection, so at least one newcomer will join the council. Councilmember Alice Fredericks, on the council since 2001 and a five-time mayor, is seeking a seventh term. Councilmember Jack Ryan, a retired derivatives trading manager first elected in a 2020 special election and mayor in 2023, is seeking a second full term. The challengers are Planning Commissioner Kathleen Defever, an attorney who lost council bids in 2020 and 2021; Chuck Hornbrook, a member of the Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission who ran fourth in 2024; and Faris Jafar, founder of the wealth-management firm Jafar Management and a member of the Reed district’s budget advisory committee.

item.title: Nine-townhome plan for Point Tiburon clears key hurdle after three rejections
item.description: Tiburon deemed Black Oak Ventures’ fourth application for nine townhomes on the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot complete Oct. 22; the town must decide by Nov. 23.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon deemed Black Oak Ventures’ fourth application for nine townhomes on the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot complete Oct. 22; the town must decide by Nov. 23.

After three failed submissions over the past year, a Berkeley developer has cleared a major hurdle to build nine townhomes on part of the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot.

Tiburon notified Black Oak Ventures Oct. 22 that the fourth version of its 1801 Tiburon Blvd. application is complete. The town now has until Nov. 23, 60 days after Black Oak filed that version Sept. 24, to approve or deny the project, Tiburon Senior Planner Kristin Teiche has said.

“We are pleased that the town has confirmed that our application is complete and look forward to receiving the approval of the application within weeks,” Black Oak founder and principal owner Michael Yarne said Oct. 23.

Yarne’s firm is working with Point Tiburon Plaza owner Chong Cook to subdivide part of the parking lot into nine lots for detached three-story townhomes, each with a two-car garage and partial storage cellar.

Black Oak filed the project under Senate Bill 684, the 2023 Starter Home Revitalization Act, which requires staff-level approval of housing projects of 10 homes or fewer that meet objective standards, with no public hearings or discretionary review.

Under Senate Bill 684, the town can deny a qualifying project only if it finds in writing that the project would have a specific, adverse impact on public health or safety that cannot be feasibly mitigated. Town officials have said Tiburon can attach conditions of approval.

item.title: Tiburon sailor’s America’s Cup campaign reaches the big screen
item.description: “Mighty Mary,” a new documentary about the 1995 all-women America’s Cup crew, recounts the campaign of Tiburon’s Melissa Purdy Feagin, the boat’s mainsail trimmer.
item.content:encoded:
“Mighty Mary,” a new documentary about the 1995 all-women America’s Cup crew, recounts the campaign of Tiburon’s Melissa Purdy Feagin, the boat’s mainsail trimmer.

More than three decades after Tiburon resident Melissa Purdy Feagin helped propel the first all-woman America’s Cup team through one of the world’s most prestigious competitions, she is watching the story of Mighty Mary reach a new audience.

“Mighty Mary,” a new feature-length documentary, recounts the 1995 campaign in which the crew competed for the right to defend the America’s Cup. Feagin, then Melissa Purdy, was the boat’s mainsail trimmer, controlling the sail’s shape and tension to help keep the 55,000-pound yacht moving at top speed.

The 98-minute documentary, directed by former Olympic rower Mary Mazzio and narrated by actors Hugh Jackman and Elizabeth Banks, opened in select theaters nationwide Sept. 11. It screens at 8 p.m. Nov. 4 and 5 at the Marina Theatre on Chestnut Street in San Francisco, where both showings are scheduled to include Q&A sessions with members of the film’s cast. Feagin plans to attend the Nov. 5 screening.

The film revisits a campaign in which Mighty Mary took on teams led by some of the most experienced sailors in America’s Cup history and nearly advanced to defend the trophy before a series of internal conflicts, personnel changes and competition decisions altered its course.

item.title: Reed Union schools to develop age-based framework for screens, AI
item.description: Reed Union School District board members questioned student screen time Oct. 13; a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI comes to the board in February.
item.content:encoded:
Reed Union School District board members questioned student screen time Oct. 13; a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI comes to the board in February.

Four months after approving the district’s first artificial intelligence policy, Reed Union School District board members used their first look at a districtwide technology plan to ask whether students from preschool through eighth grade spend too long on screens.

Jonathan Weller, the district’s director of information systems, educational technology and innovation, told the board Oct. 13 that a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI will come to the board in February.

Board members’ concerns surfaced minutes earlier, during an update on curriculum pilots, when board member Mike Ghaffary said classrooms should use real textbooks and paper and pencil whenever possible.

“I think the whole world has jumped the shark on overreliance on technology,” Ghaffary said.

He said it would be “a bit hypocritical” for parents, teachers and the board to warn students against device addiction outside school, then require the devices in class and at night to turn in homework.

item.title: Late filings show who’s paying for Tiburon council, fire, school races
item.description: Alice Fredericks raised the most from donors among Tiburon Town Council candidates in the last pre-election reports, while Kathleen Defever outspent the field with a loan.
item.content:encoded:
Alice Fredericks raised the most from donors among Tiburon Town Council candidates in the last pre-election reports, while Kathleen Defever outspent the field with a loan.

Incumbent Councilmember Alice Fredericks raised the most money from donors among Tiburon’s Town Council candidates in the last campaign-finance reports before the Nov. 3 election, while challenger Kathleen Defever outspent the field with money she lent her own campaign.

Fredericks reported $2,124 in monetary contributions in the period from Sept. 20 to Oct. 17, the last preelection disclosure ahead of the Nov. 3 race for three seats. She reported spending $4,457 in the period.

Planning Commissioner Defever reported the largest total, $10,850, but $9,400 of it is a loan she made to her own campaign. The other $1,450 came from donors.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Parks, Open Space & Trails Commissioner Chuck Hornbrook reported $1,662 in contributions, $1,350 of it from donors, and investment-fund founder Faris Jafar reported $1,591 in donations.

Defever also reported the most spending in the period, $8,462. Hornbrook reported $4,828 in expenditures, Fredericks $4,457 and Jafar $3,453.

The California Fair Political Practices Commission requires two campaign-finance disclosures before an election from candidates who raise or spend $2,000 or more. The first, due Sept. 24, covered July 1-Sept. 19.

The other incumbent seeking reelection, Councilmember Jack Ryan, did not need to submit a campaign-finance report, as he filed a statement Sept. 16 saying he expects to receive and spend less than $2,000 this year.

Elsewhere on peninsula ballots, firefighter unions put money behind two Southern Marin Fire Protection District challengers, and a new committee reported spending against Marin County Board of Education incumbent Marilyn Nemzer.

Defever received $500 each from Tiburon resident Hank McWhinney and part-time Strawberry resident Priya Clemens, $250 from Tiburon attorney Jon Rankin and $100 each from Tiburon residents John B. Snell and Belle Guelden. She lent her campaign the $9,400 on Oct. 4 and another $5,600 on Oct. 23, according to 24-hour reports she filed Oct. 22 and Oct. 26.

item.title: Developer agrees to pay Strawberry neighbors $100,000 to end senior-housing suit
item.description: Spirit Living Group will pay Tiburon Ridge Neighbors $100,000 to end their suit over its shelved Strawberry senior-housing complex; it remains free to apply again.
item.content:encoded:
Spirit Living Group will pay Tiburon Ridge Neighbors $100,000 to end their suit over its shelved Strawberry senior-housing complex; it remains free to apply again.

The developer of a shelved senior-housing complex on a Strawberry hillside has agreed to pay neighbors who sued over it $100,000 to end the case, under a settlement that leaves the company free to apply again and the neighbors free to challenge it.

Spirit Living Group agreed to pay the 60-member Tiburon Ridge Neighbors and its leader, Scott Arwin, $100,000 for legal expenses and costs, according to a copy of the settlement agreement Marin County Counsel Brandon Halter provided to The Ark Oct. 19. Apart from that payment, each party covers its own attorney fees and costs.

The county, whose December approval the neighbors challenged, is a party to the settlement but paid nothing, Halter said.

The county and Spirit Living signed the agreement Sept. 24 and 25, and the neighbors notified the court of the settlement Sept. 28. The agreement required them to ask the court to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning the claims cannot be refiled, and the case was dismissed Oct. 8, court records show.

But the deal covers only the county’s Dec. 23 approval, which the county voided in June at the developer’s request. It “does not bar any challenge to any future application” for the 100 Thomas Place parcels, and it does not bind any party on a future project at the same site. No party admits liability.

Arwin and the neighbors’ attorney, Richard Drury, did not respond to multiple requests for comment by The Ark’s press deadline, nor did Sarah Ellen Owsowitz, an attorney for Spirit Living. Spirit Living co-owner Ali Shabahangi and Riley Hurd, who has also represented the company, did not respond to a request sent Oct. 20.

No new application has been filed for the site, county Senior Planner Megan Alton said Oct. 14.

item.title: Octogenarian Marin rowing crew with Tiburon’s Kim Coggan takes on Head of the Charles
item.description: Tiburon’s Kim Coggan and her Marin Rowing Association crew, average age 80, raced the Head of the Charles in Boston Oct. 17, finishing nearly three minutes faster than expected.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon’s Kim Coggan and her Marin Rowing Association crew, average age 80, raced the Head of the Charles in Boston Oct. 17, finishing nearly three minutes faster than expected.

At 77, Tiburon resident Kim Coggan cannot power a racing shell the way she once did. Her crew’s stroke rate has slowed, and recovery requires more attention. But on Oct. 17 on the Charles River in Boston, Coggan and seven longtime teammates raced the course in a little more than 27 minutes, nearly three minutes faster than they had expected.

The Marin Rowing Association crew, which club members say was the first women’s eight with an average age of 80 to race the Head of the Charles Regatta, finished in 27 minutes, 6 seconds, in the regatta’s women’s veteran eights.

The crew finished last of 25 in a field made up mostly of crews in their 60s, the only boat in the 80-and-older category.

“We knew that what we had to do was recognize our strengths,” Coggan said. “We don’t have the power that younger crews do, but we can row well together.”

The women settled into a pace of about 24 or 25 strokes per minute, down from the 28 to 30 or more they might have maintained while racing in their 60s and 70s. Rather than trying to match younger competitors stroke for stroke, they concentrated on their technique and cohesion.

“We raced our own race,” Coggan said. “I’m very pleased with our finish.”

item.title: An Australian transplant builds a life in Tiburon
item.description: Tiburon resident Jill Kantola, who grew up in Perth, Australia, says the schools, scenery and friendliness of the community persuaded her family to stay.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Jill Kantola, who grew up in Perth, Australia, says the schools, scenery and friendliness of the community persuaded her family to stay.

Rain dots the pavement on the afternoon of Oct. 21 as Tiburon resident Jill Kantola walks her dog, Billie, through Shoreline Park. It’s a routine that brings her regularly to the Tiburon waterfront.

Billie spends plenty of time outdoors, Kantola says, and their walks offer a chance to enjoy the waterfront, one of the features that has kept her in Tiburon for 31 years.

“It’s so beautiful,” she says.

“I walk her up here every day,” Kantola says.

Kantola and her husband, Steve, raised two children in Tiburon, where they attended Reed and Del Mar schools. She says the schools, scenery and friendliness of the community helped persuade the family to stay.

“The school districts were great, people are friendly,” Kantola says. “I love living here. I don’t want to move.”

item.content:encoded:
John Harrington, 87, a longtime Marin County resident, passed away peacefully at his home in Tiburon on October 8, 2026.

Born in Minnesota on May 31, 1939, John attended the University of Minnesota before moving to California, where he earned his MBA from UCLA. He began his career as a certified public accountant with Price Waterhouse (now PricewaterhouseCoopers) in Beverly Hills. In 1973, he transferred to the firm’s San Francisco office and moved to Tiburon with his family.

Throughout his career, John served as chief financial officer for numerous companies, supported startups, and advised families on financial planning, family trusts, and wealth transfers. Known for his generosity, thoughtfulness, and intellect, John was especially generous with his time, knowledge, and resources, always willing to help individuals and businesses navigate challenges and pursue opportunities.

In 2000, John met Ida Baugh, and they married in Sausalito in 2005. They made their home together in Tiburon in 2007, where John lived for the remainder of his life.

John is survived by his wife, Ida Baugh of Tiburon; his son, Bradford Harrington of Milwaukee, Wisconsin; his daughter, Laurel Harrington of Mill Valley, California; his stepson, Christopher Baugh of Wellesley, Massachusetts; and his stepdaughter, Whitney Peters of Tiburon, California.

A celebration of John’s life will be held at a later date.

In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in John’s memory to Sutter Care at Home: https://give.sutterhealth.org/campaign/723377/donate.

item.title: ‘We shouldn’t be here’: Family, friends mourn Strawberry’s Ann Mannix and daughter Katie at San Francisco funeral
item.description: Family, friends and police packed St. Ignatius Church in San Francisco Oct. 23 for the funeral of Strawberry residents Ann Mannix and her daughter, Katie Mannix.
item.content:encoded:
Family, friends and police packed St. Ignatius Church in San Francisco Oct. 23 for the funeral of Strawberry residents Ann Mannix and her daughter, Katie Mannix.

Family, friends, law enforcement and government officials packed St. Ignatius Church in San Francisco Oct. 23 for the funeral Mass of Strawberry resident Ann Mannix, a former deputy chief at the San Francisco Police Department.

Mannix, 65, and daughter Katherine “Katie” Mannix, 24, were killed Oct. 11 in their Strawberry home by Mannix’s husband, 68-year-old retired SFPD Sgt. Kevin Mannix Sr., who then killed himself, according to the Marin County Sheriff’s Office’s preliminary findings.

Richard Corriea, Ann Mannix’s brother, called the killings a “brutal, horrible act of violence.”

Corriea and Katie’s siblings, Lauren and Kevin Jr., described Mannix as a fantastic mother who supported her children in their struggles and made life more vibrant, on top of her accolades in law enforcement and her qualities as a friend and athlete.

Katie’s siblings described her as a smart and kind person who always looked to improve the world around her.

“We shouldn’t be here,” Corriea said.

Mannix, a Strawberry resident since 1989, joined the San Francisco Police Department in 1986 and retired in 2021 as a deputy chief, the department’s highest-ranking woman, The Ark reported when she retired. She earned a political science degree from Loyola Marymount University, where she played center on its basketball team.

Corriea, a retired SFPD commander, chronicled his sister’s life, from his first memory, the day she came home from the hospital Feb. 14, 1961, two days after she was born, to convincing their father to start making them sugar-sprinkled bacon instead of Spam, to growing up together.

“I’m blessed for that, at this time, at the time of her death, we were at a perigee: in contact daily and making time for seeing one another,” Corriea said.

Kevin Mannix Jr. recalled taking his mother to a San Francisco 49ers game in 2020. She kept thanking him for taking her to the game, he said, but there was no one else “on this planet I would rather spend a day screaming, cheering, high-fiving and hugging with.”

item.title: A&C Ventures revives downtown Tiburon housing plan with 127 units
item.description: A&C Ventures has revived its plan to build housing on three Tiburon Boulevard properties, now proposing 127 rental units with 20 reserved for lower-income tenants.
item.content:encoded:
A&C Ventures has revived its plan to build housing on three Tiburon Boulevard properties, now proposing 127 rental units with 20 reserved for lower-income tenants.

Downtown landlord A&C Ventures has revived its plan to build housing on three Tiburon Boulevard properties, now proposing 127 rental units with 20 reserved for lower-income tenants.

The company announced Oct. 22 that it had submitted two preliminary applications to the town for the same three sites it targeted nearly two years ago: the old Bank of America and Shark’s Deli sites and the parking lot next to Town Hall.

The residential-only plan, from the Sonoma-based company, which does business locally as ACV Argo Tiburon LP, and San Diego-based developer Naturally Affordable Housing, would put 77 units on the old bank site and its parking lot at 1601 Tiburon Blvd. and 4 Beach Road; 19 across Tiburon Boulevard at 1600 Tiburon Blvd.; and 31 on the lot next to Town Hall at 1525 Tiburon Blvd.

It is the company’s second try. A&C Ventures filed a preliminary application for 120 units in December 2024 but did not follow it with a formal application by the June 2025 deadline. The new plan raises the number of lower-income units to 20, up from eight, and the parking to 197 spaces, up from 163.

Tiburon’s housing element, the state-required plan for meeting its share of regional housing need, counts on the same four parcels for 79 units, 64 of them for lower-income households. A&C’s plan would build 48 more units than that projection but 44 fewer for lower incomes, 36 of them in the very-low-income category.

Under state no-net-loss law, if Tiburon approves a project with fewer units in an income category than its housing element projected for a parcel, it must make written findings on whether its remaining sites can still meet its share of the regional need. That share includes 193 very-low-income and 110 low-income units in the 2023-2031 housing cycle. If the remaining sites fall short, the town has 180 days to identify and make available new ones. The law bars the town from denying a project on that basis.

Robert Brown, A&C Ventures’ senior vice president of real estate, said in an Oct. 22 news release, provided exclusively to The Ark, that the company wants to create opportunities for the local workforce “to live closer to where they work.”

item.title: Belvedere considers water-filled flood barriers as El Niño threat grows
item.description: Belvedere may line San Rafael Avenue and Beach Road with water-filled flood barriers this winter as forecasters warn a very strong El Niño could bring flooding.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere may line San Rafael Avenue and Beach Road with water-filled flood barriers this winter as forecasters warn a very strong El Niño could bring flooding.

Belvedere may line San Rafael Avenue and Beach Road with water-filled flood barriers this winter, a stopgap meant to hold back a 50-year flood as forecasters warn a very strong El Niño and king tides could collide over the holidays.

Public Works Director Antony Boyd outlined the plan Oct. 12 in a winter-preparedness report to the City Council, saying the city is working with Stetson Engineers to design a temporary barrier system for the two roads, which carry the city’s utilities and form the edges of the Belvedere Lagoon.

The effort is in its preliminary stage, Boyd said, and the exact design is still being worked out. Staff expects to return with an update and possible council action Nov. 9.

The federal Climate Prediction Center said Oct. 8 that El Niño continues to strengthen and that a strong to very strong event is likely to last through January-March 2027. It put the chance at 83% that October-December brings a historic event, exceeding any El Niño since 1950 at 4.5 degrees Fahrenheit or more above normal on a three-month Relative Oceanic Niño Index. Its next update is due Nov. 12.

“For a community like Belvedere with significantly low-lying areas and waterfront infrastructure, that is something that we need to take seriously,” City Manager Robert Zadnik said in introducing the item.

item.title: Belvedere’s Mallard Pointe apartments coming down
item.description: Demolition of Belvedere’s 22-unit Mallard Pointe apartments began Oct. 15 to make way for a 40-unit development; an appeal of its bulkhead permits is set for Nov. 9.
item.content:encoded:
Demolition of Belvedere’s 22-unit Mallard Pointe apartments began Oct. 15 to make way for a 40-unit development; an appeal of its bulkhead permits is set for Nov. 9.

An excavator carries debris to a dumpster at Mallard Pointe in Belvedere on Oct. 16. Demolition of the 22-unit Mallard Road apartment complex, which is being replaced by a 40-unit development, began along the shoreline Oct. 15 so developer Thompson Dorfman LLC may begin in-water bulkhead work in the Belvedere Lagoon. The developer must install a shoreline silt fence shown in the approved plans, or get an alternative approved, and add a second, full-depth turbidity curtain before the bulkhead work starts. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife has allowed lagoon work through Oct. 22, and the developer plans to seek more time. The City Council is scheduled Nov. 9 to hear a residents’ group’s appeal of the project’s bulkhead permits.

item.title: Belvedere shelves rules for drone deliveries after resident backlash
item.description: Belvedere has shelved its proposed rules for commercial drone deliveries and will pursue a regional approach with other Marin cities after weeks of resident opposition.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere has shelved its proposed rules for commercial drone deliveries and will pursue a regional approach with other Marin cities after weeks of resident opposition.

Belvedere has temporarily shelved its proposed rules for commercial drone deliveries and plans to work out an approach with other Marin towns and cities after weeks of resident opposition that included calls for an outright ban.

Mayor Sally Wilkinson pulled the ordinance’s second reading, the vote that would have adopted it, at the start of the City Council’s Oct. 12 meeting. The council took public comment on the item but did not discuss it or vote. No date has been set for its return, though Wilkinson said at the meeting it would come back “at some point.”

After reviewing a first draft July 13 and sending it back for revisions, councilmembers narrowly approved the revised ordinance on first reading 3-2 on Sept. 14, with Councilmembers Jane Cooper and Pat Carapiet opposed over its delivery hours. That set up the adoption vote last week.

Wilkinson explained the decision in a statement she wrote for the city’s Oct. 16 Belvedere Breeze newsletter.

“The city’s authority is largely limited to ground operations, and we don’t want to promise protections we cannot legally deliver,” she said. “We’re now exploring a regional approach with other Marin communities and look forward to continuing the conversation with residents as we learn more about this emerging industry.”

item.title: Tiburon faces Oct. 24 deadline on latest Point Tiburon housing plan
item.description: Tiburon has until Oct. 24 to decide whether Black Oak Ventures’ fourth application for nine townhomes on the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot is complete.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon has until Oct. 24 to decide whether Black Oak Ventures’ fourth application for nine townhomes on the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot is complete.

Tiburon has until Oct. 24 to decide whether a Berkeley developer’s fourth application to build nine townhomes on the Point Tiburon Plaza parking lot is complete.

Black Oak Ventures filed the latest version of its 1801 Tiburon Blvd. application the evening of Sept. 24, starting the town’s 30-day review.

If the application is complete, the town will have until Nov. 23, 60 days from when it was submitted, to approve or deny the project, town senior planner Kristin Teiche said.

The town can also impose conditions of approval, Teiche said.

The project is proposed under Senate Bill 684, the 2023 Starter Home Revitalization Act. The law requires ministerial approval of qualifying small housing projects that meet objective standards, without public hearings or discretionary review. It applies to developments of 10 homes or fewer.

item.title: Reed Union student test scores remain steady for English, math
item.description: Reed Union School District students held steady on the 2025-2026 state tests, with 80.7% meeting English standards and 78.8% in math, well above Marin and the state.
item.content:encoded:
Reed Union School District students held steady on the 2025-2026 state tests, with 80.7% meeting English standards and 78.8% in math, well above Marin and the state.

Reed Union School District students held steady on the state’s English and math tests in 2025-2026 and continued to outscore students across Marin County and California by wide margins.

Some 80.7% of Reed district students met or exceeded grade-level standards in English and 78.8% did the same in math on the California Assessment of Student Performance and Progress, according to results the state released Oct. 15. Both figures were essentially unchanged from 2024-2025, when 80.9% and 78.9% met the mark. The district’s socioeconomically disadvantaged students lost ground, falling to 37.8% in English from about 53%.

Statewide, 49.3% of students met or exceeded standards on the English test and 38.4% in math, up 0.5 and 1.1 percentage points, respectively. Marin students performed better than the state average, with 61.8% meeting or exceeding standards in English and 54.5% doing so in math.

item.title: Belvedere weighs police merger with Tiburon or regional agency
item.description: Belvedere is preparing to hire a firm to study its Police Department, including whether to merge or share policing with Tiburon; a contract could come in November.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere is preparing to hire a firm to study its Police Department, including whether to merge or share policing with Tiburon; a contract could come in November.

Belvedere is preparing to hire an outside firm to study whether the city should keep its own Police Department or share policing with Tiburon, through a merger, a shared police chief or a joint agency the two cities would govern together.

City Manager Robert Zadnik told the City Council on Oct. 12 that the study would come in two parts. The first would examine the existing department, including its staffing, equipment and overall operations.

“The first part of that firm’s work will focus on our current operations, including whether our staffing levels and equipment are appropriate for the department in a community of our size,” Zadnik said.

The second would take a longer look at the department’s future, including whether it is feasible to consolidate police services with Tiburon or form a joint police agency.

“That’s something that’s long been thought about, but never fully researched,” he said.

item.title: Strawberry Recreation District board advances trimmed Strawberry Park playground design at $2.55 million
item.description: A trimmed design cuts Strawberry Park’s planned playground and soccer field to about $2.55 million; the Strawberry Recreation District board takes a final vote Nov. 10.
item.content:encoded:
A trimmed design cuts Strawberry Park’s planned playground and soccer field to about $2.55 million; the Strawberry Recreation District board takes a final vote Nov. 10.

A trimmed-down design has cut the price of Strawberry’s planned playground and soccer field to about $2.55 million, roughly $50,000 above the $2.5 million cap the Strawberry Recreation District board set in September.

The board voted 4-0 on Oct. 13, with Chair Peter Teese absent, to have the general manager send playground company GameTime a letter of intent. Final approval of the playground waits for the board’s Nov. 10 meeting so all five members can vote.

The play area centers on a large red strawberry that children can slide down. It will sit on a patch of grass between the tennis courts and baseball fields at Strawberry Park, atop a rubber surface decorated with strawberry vines. GameTime’s quote in the board’s Oct. 13 meeting packet says equipment ships within 24 weeks after the company receives a signed quote, purchase order and color selections, which would mean by late April for an order placed right after the Nov. 10 vote.

item.title: Redwood student launches inclusive tennis program at Strawberry Recreation District
item.description: Redwood High School junior Jonah Bilsker launched an ACEing Autism adaptive tennis program Oct. 3 at Strawberry Recreation District.
item.content:encoded:
Redwood High School junior Jonah Bilsker launched an ACEing Autism adaptive tennis program Oct. 3 at Strawberry Recreation District.

Jonah Bilsker first volunteered with an adaptive tennis program for children with autism in Los Gatos, among the closest to home. On Oct. 3 the Redwood High School junior opened Marin’s first on the upper courts at Strawberry Recreation District.

The program, run by the national nonprofit ACEing Autism, is a six-week series of classes that aims to help young athletes build tennis, motor and social skills.

Bilsker, a varsity tennis player, organized it with his mother, Ross resident Avi Downes, and serves as its on-court director.

Twelve high school volunteers and six young athletes turned out for the first class. Ten athletes had registered, but the heat kept some home. Volunteers fed balls to the athletes, who practiced forehands and backhands, and the session ended with a game of red light, green light.

item.title: Tiburon OKs boutique fitness studio for long-vacant storefront next to CVS
item.description: Tiburon’s Planning Commission approved Pelican Pro Fitness, a boutique studio, for the long-vacant storefront next to CVS at 1599 Tiburon Blvd.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon’s Planning Commission approved Pelican Pro Fitness, a boutique studio, for the long-vacant storefront next to CVS at 1599 Tiburon Blvd.

A boutique fitness studio will fill the long-vacant storefront next to the CVS/pharmacy in downtown Tiburon, the second fitness business the Planning Commission has approved in as many months.

The commission voted 4-0 on Oct. 14 to let Pelican Pro Fitness open a 1,800-square-foot studio at 1599 Tiburon Blvd., with Commissioner Jeff Tsai absent. No one spoke during public comment.

Owner Nick Price, who is also the CEO of Price Family Dealerships, which his parents, Tom and Gwen Price, own, told The Ark after the meeting he aims to open as soon as the town’s permitting process allows. He told commissioners he subleases the space from CVS and has held the lease for some time. The building’s owner, Zelinsky Properties, which also owns Ark Row and other downtown buildings, signed off on the sublease, Nick Price said.

The membership- and appointment-based studio will offer one-on-one personal training and limited weekly group classes from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily, within the hours of the CVS store next door, which is open 7 a.m.-10 p.m. Mondays-Saturdays and 7 a.m.-9 p.m. Sundays.

item.title: Tiburon Town Council candidates differ on parks funding, term limits, Flock, AI
item.description: Tiburon Town Council candidates split on private park money, term limits and AI in follow-up interviews, but all five were open to a hearing on Flock cameras.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Town Council candidates split on private park money, term limits and AI in follow-up interviews, but all five were open to a hearing on Flock cameras.

Tiburon Town Council candidates differed on private money for parks, term limits and artificial intelligence in follow-up interviews with The Ark, though all five said they were open to a public hearing on the town’s Flock license-plate cameras.

Kathleen Defever, Alice Fredericks, Chuck Hornbrook, Faris Jafar and Jack Ryan answered questions over the past two weeks that the Sept. 29 candidate forum, hosted by The Ark and moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County, did not have time to reach.

Defever, Hornbrook and Jafar are each seeking their first term on the council. Ryan, on the council since winning a 2020 special election, is seeking his second full term, while Fredericks is seeking a seventh term after being first elected in 2001.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The five candidates are vying for three seats in the Nov. 3 election. The winners will serve four-year terms that end November 2030.

At the candidate forum, candidates mostly agreed that residents should help oversee town finances but were split on the town’s use of Flock license-plate cameras, housing approaches and paying for parks.

The follow-up interviews also covered which park projects to build first, community resiliency, term limits, artificial intelligence and civic engagement.

Candidates differed on seeking private contributions for the parks on top of public money and on how to decide what gets built if the town cannot afford every project at once.

Total costs for the revamped Bel Aire play area, which is under construction, are estimated at $1.02 million, and the projected construction cost of a park at the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green has climbed to $3.7 million. Town officials are also scaling back a redesign of Cypress Hollow Park, aiming to cut its $2.5 million price tag at least in half.

The next council will also have to decide how to proceed if the planned projects together prove too expensive. The town has not decided how to pay for the ponds park, and the earliest voters could approve a tax or bond for it is November 2028.

item.title: Resident group says Belvedere issued Mallard Pointe permits prematurely
item.description: Belvedere Residents for Intelligent Growth has appealed Mallard Pointe bulkhead permits; the City Council will hear the appeal Nov. 9, and work continues meanwhile.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere Residents for Intelligent Growth has appealed Mallard Pointe bulkhead permits; the City Council will hear the appeal Nov. 9, and work continues meanwhile.

Belvedere Residents for Intelligent Growth has appealed the city’s Mallard Pointe bulkhead permits, arguing they were issued before required geotechnical and flood-plain reviews were done. The city has said it can’t halt work while the appeal waits for a City Council hearing.

The group, formed in 2021 to fight the 40-home redevelopment, filed the appeal Oct. 6, five days after the city issued the two permits for tearing out and replacing the shoreline bulkhead along the Belvedere Lagoon edge of the 1-22 Mallard Road site. It asks the council to rescind or suspend the permits and stop bulkhead work until the steps it says are missing are done.

The council will hear the appeal Nov. 9, or earlier if possible, the city said in an Oct. 12 update to residents.

In an Oct. 9 letter to the group’s attorney, City Manager Robert Zadnik said the city could not grant the request to stop work in the meantime. Under the state building code the city has adopted, the building official may suspend a permit only if it was “issued in error or on the basis of incorrect, inaccurate or incomplete information, or in violation of any ordinance or regulation,” Zadnik said, citing the code, and an appeal alone is not grounds.

“The building official does not believe that any of these circumstances apply in the instant case,” he said.

item.title: Belvedere resident sues Tiburon, police officers over alleged wrongful arrest, privacy violations
item.description: A Belvedere resident is suing Tiburon and three police officers, alleging an arrest without probable cause on an October 2025 domestic-violence call.
item.content:encoded:
A Belvedere resident is suing Tiburon and three police officers, alleging an arrest without probable cause on an October 2025 domestic-violence call.

A Belvedere resident is suing the town of Tiburon and three police officers, saying officers arrested her without probable cause on a domestic-violence call in October 2025 and refused to let her dress before taking her to jail.

Veronika Van Den Top, who lived in Tiburon at the time of her arrest, filed the civil suit Sept. 22 in Marin County Superior Court and is seeking a jury trial. She alleges that police Sgt. Freddy Gutierrez and Officer James Harris violated her civil rights by arresting her without probable cause.

The Marin County District Attorney’s Office did not file a criminal complaint over the arrest, said Alfiya Nachtigall, an administrative secretary for the office.

In a separate family-court case, a Superior Court judge denied requests by Van Den Top and her husband for longer-term domestic-violence restraining orders against each other Feb. 27 after a contested hearing, court records show.

item.title: Assembly Democrats Lucan, Elward agree on policy, spar over outside money
item.description: Assembly candidates Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward agreed on most policy at a Sept. 30 forum but sparred over millions in outside money in the 12th District race.
item.content:encoded:
Assembly candidates Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward agreed on most policy at a Sept. 30 forum but sparred over millions in outside money in the 12th District race.

The two Democrats competing to succeed Assemblymember Damon Connolly agreed on most policy questions at an online candidate forum, but Marin Supervisor Eric Lucan and Rohnert Park Councilmember Jackie Elward sparred over the millions in outside money flooding their race.

The Sept. 30 webinar was hosted by the Coalition of Sensible Taxpayers, a Marin taxpayer-advocacy group, and moderated by Marin Independent Journal columnist Dick Spotswood.

Both candidates said they support state funding to finish high-speed rail, oppose Proposition 43, which would make local tax measures put on the ballot by citizen initiative harder to pass, and would have backed a police and firefighter pension bill Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed last month. Lucan’s answers centered on financing tools for housing, Elward’s on local control and accountability for state spending.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The 12th Assembly District covers all of Marin County and part of Sonoma County, including Rohnert Park and a portion of Petaluma. Connolly, D-San Rafael, is running for the state Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Mike McGuire, who is termed out.

Lucan, a former three-term Novato councilmember and mayor elected to the Board of Supervisors in 2022, led the six-candidate June 2 primary with 28.3%. Elward, a former Rohnert Park mayor and an educator who came to the U.S. from the Democratic Republic of Congo, was second at 22.6%. Under California’s top-two system, the two highest vote-getters advance regardless of party.

Tiburon Councilmember Holli Thier, the only candidate from the peninsula, finished fourth at 14% and conceded in June. Lucan led on the Tiburon Peninsula in early returns, with 28.7% of the 4,712 votes counted at the time, ahead of Thier at 23.6%.

Spotswood asked each candidate how big money would affect their decisions in Sacramento. He said Lucan had received $551,000 in September from Grow California, a political action committee founded by tech and cryptocurrency billionaires Tim Draper and Chris Larsen.

Lucan said that was wrong.

item.title: State Senate candidates Connolly, Gibbs clash over taxes, housing, homelessness
item.description: State Senate candidates Damon Connolly and Tief Gibbs split over Marin’s childcare tax, homelessness and a statewide tax measure, but both vowed to rein in state housing laws.
item.content:encoded:
State Senate candidates Damon Connolly and Tief Gibbs split over Marin’s childcare tax, homelessness and a statewide tax measure, but both vowed to rein in state housing laws.

The two Marin residents vying to succeed termed-out state Sen. Mike McGuire split over Marin’s childcare parcel tax, homelessness and a statewide measure to make citizen-initiated local taxes harder to pass, though both pledged to rein in state housing laws.

Assemblymember Damon Connolly, D-San Rafael, and Republican Tief Gibbs of Novato answered questions for more than an hour Sept. 24 in an online forum hosted by the Coalition of Sensible Taxpayers, a Marin taxpayer-advocacy group Connolly thanked for endorsing him in his 2022 Assembly race. Marin Independent Journal columnist Dick Spotswood moderated.

The 2nd State Senate District, which includes the Tiburon Peninsula, runs from the Golden Gate Bridge to the Oregon border, taking in Del Norte, Humboldt, Lake, Marin, Mendocino and Trinity counties and part of Sonoma. McGuire, a Democrat and former Senate president pro tem, is running for Congress in the 1st District.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Both candidates said they would roll back or rewrite state housing laws that override local zoning.

Connolly is a former Marin supervisor, San Rafael councilmember and state deputy attorney general who has represented Marin in the Assembly since 2022. He said he had not supported Senate Bill 79, the 2025 law that took effect July 1 and allows apartment buildings of five to nine stories within a half-mile of major transit stations in urban counties, or Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131, 2025 budget bills that loosened state environmental review for infill housing. He voted against SB 79 and did not vote on final passage of AB 130 or SB 131. All three became law.

He also took aim at the regional housing needs allocation, the state process that sets how many homes each city and county must plan for, saying it assigns numbers within deadlines “that don’t really make sense.” He said the idea of revisiting it has met “a chilly reception so far” among his colleagues.

item.title: Tiburon faces $1.6 million annual gap in road maintenance funding
item.description: Tiburon has about five years of dedicated pavement money left before it would need roughly $1.6 million a year from its general fund to keep up road work.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon has about five years of dedicated pavement money left before it would need roughly $1.6 million a year from its general fund to keep up road work.

Tiburon has five years’ worth of funding left for pavement-focused projects before it must dip into its general fund to keep up the same level of maintenance, according to one town official.

Public Works Operations & Technology Manager Patrick Kerslake gave the update Oct. 7 in a “State of the Pavement” presentation to the Town Council. He said the town could need about $1.6 million a year from its general fund to keep spending at current levels once its restricted road reserves run out.

“Basically, the trend reflects a structural funding gap between the town’s desired pavement investment and condition level, and the amount supported by recurring restricted transportation revenues,” Kerslake said.
